role: On-site food safety officer at a university canteen
headline: The on-site catering food safety officer in a university canteen in Nanjing's Jiangning university town, run by a contract catering company: in the kitchen at half past five every morning for health checks, retained samples and temperatures, guarding three meals a day for twenty thousand students
unit: A Nanjing contract catering company running more than a dozen canteens at seven universities in the Jiangning and Xianlin university towns
education: Associate degree, vocational college (food quality and safety)
level: You've just passed the training and assessment for food safety management staff. You can complete the daily control checklist on your own and know how to take samples, temperatures and disinfectant concentrations. Saying no to a fifty-year-old head chef, you still stumble over the words
intro: You've spent a year in the kitchens of this university canteen, going from helping copy out temperature logs to completing a full daily control checklist on your own. The canteen serves more than twenty thousand meals a day: three floors, forty-odd serving windows, over a hundred staff. As of today, you are the one person in this canteen whose job is to say: this doesn't go out.
salary_note: Estimate: an on-site safety officer for a Nanjing contract caterer, base pay plus a site allowance, earns a little above the national figure. Over winter and summer breaks, with the students gone and only one window open, some months pay just the base salary.

facts.label: Catering Food Safety Officer (current level)
facts.value: 1-3 years, ¥4,590–6,750 a month (national average, estimated from pay by experience)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Handling a customer complaint of suspected food poisoning

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Doing the daily kitchen control check before lunch service

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: It's still dark, and the early-shift pastry cook is already kneading dough. You stand at the changing-room door doing health checks: looking at hands for cuts, asking about diarrhea and fever, ticking each person off in the health register.

The cold-chain truck arrives. You climb into the back and push a probe thermometer into a case of frozen chicken legs: minus fifteen. Then you go through the supplier's quarantine certificate and delivery note, and only after you sign can they unload.
Breakfast opens. You take one each of the steamed buns, soy milk and eggs for the retained samples, weigh out a full 125 grams, label them with date and meal, and put them in the sample fridge.

You test the disinfectant in the dishwashing room with a strip, and the color is pale. The woman washing dishes says she just mixed it. You ask her to mix it again and stand beside her while she measures.

The tightest stretch is before lunch. You stab the braised pork and the fish with a core thermometer, releasing nothing below seventy degrees; at the door of the cold-dish room you watch the cooks change a second time, wash and sanitize their hands before going in.

A student leaves a message in the canteen's mini-app: a hair in the rice on the second floor. You pull up the open-kitchen camera footage, find the server whose cap wasn't on properly, and talk separately to him and his shift lead.

Afternoon is the weekly inspection. You crouch in the corner of the storeroom checking glue traps, look under the shelves, hunt for expired seasonings, write three items on the inspection form and post photos to the corrective-action group chat.

Dinner is done. You enter today's daily control records into the system and check the sample fridge temperature once more. Riding your e-bike home past a duck blood vermicelli soup shop at the campus gate, you buy a bowl for dinner.

ladder.title: Restaurant Kitchen / Store Management Team Member
ladder.focus: Follow the operating procedures, handle hygiene and record-keeping.

ladder.title: Catering Food Safety Officer
ladder.focus: Pass the training and assessment, run the daily controls and weekly inspections, and manage temperature control, disinfection and records.

ladder.title: Regional Food Safety Supervisor
ladder.focus: Inspect multiple sites, handle complaints and incidents, and audit suppliers.

ladder.title: Catering Food Safety Director
ladder.focus: A post large and medium catering companies are required to have: oversee the whole system and report at the monthly review.

ladder.title: Head of Quality, Catering Chain
ladder.focus: The person responsible for the group's quality and food safety system.

ai_tasks.name: Doing the daily kitchen control check before lunch service
ai_tasks.how: AI can generate the checklist, automatically compile temperature and disinfectant concentration records and flag abnormal data. A person has to be on site to see how the staff are doing, smell and look at the food, test concentrations, check samples and the separation of raw and cooked, and sign for the result.

ai_tasks.name: Receiving a delivery of cold-chain ingredients
ai_tasks.how: AI can check automatically whether the supplier's certificates have expired, whether shelf life is compliant and whether temperature data is out of range, and generate the receiving record. A person takes the temperature at the truck, checks packaging and appearance, decides whether to accept, and handles the conversation when it's a rejection.

ai_tasks.name: Running the weekly inspection and fixing hazards in the dishwashing room
ai_tasks.how: AI can generate an inspection form for the theme, summarize past problems, track and remind on corrective actions. A person goes into the dishwashing room to check the sterilizing cabinet temperature, residue on dishes and signs of pests, and works with staff until the hazards are really fixed.

ai_tasks.name: Handling a customer complaint of suspected food poisoning
ai_tasks.how: AI can help put together the timeline, apply the steps of the emergency plan and draft the incident statement and records. But sealing the retained samples, calming the customer, working with the regulators, judging responsibility and handling the scene are for a person to do and answer for.

ai_tasks.name: Keeping refrigeration and reheating under control in the summer heat
ai_tasks.how: AI can use thermometer data to tighten alerts automatically, catch refrigeration faults and cooked food held too long, and prompt reheating. A person confirms on site that equipment is running, personally checks that reheated food reaches a core temperature above 70°C, and makes sure staff follow the rules.

ai_tasks.name: Inspecting multiple sites in a region and coordinating fixes
ai_tasks.how: AI can compile inspection data from every site, score and rank them, find common problems and generate corrective notices and follow-up lists. A person visits the sites, judges what is really behind the data, and talks to managers to push the fixes through.

events.e_chef_no: You stop a batch of pork that thawed overnight and feels sticky. The head chef's face goes dark: he's been doing this thirty years. The manager comes, takes one look and has it sent back. After that, every delivery, the head chef calls you to look first.
events.e_inspection_city: The district market regulator does a surprise inspection and asks first thing for the retained sample log and staff health certificates. You find them in two minutes, and they go on to check the UV lamp records in the cold-dish room. The inspection form lists no problems.
events.e_early: Start of term, and for a month you're up at five, shuttling between the canteen and your rented room, called back on weekends to supervise the extra meals for military training. At month's end you sleep past your stop on the metro.
events.e_summer_cold: Nanjing summers are hot and close, and company rules stop cold dishes once summer starts. Students complain in the rating system for a month. You put up a notice at the canteen entrance explaining why.
events.e_burn: Checking temperatures in the hot kitchen, you're splashed on the back of the hand by spitting oil. A cook dabs some badger oil on it and says the safety officer needs to be safe too.
events.e_student_committee: The university's student catering committee tours the kitchen, and a girl asks why the cutting boards come in five colors. You explain each one, and afterward she says she'll feel better eating here now.
events.e_love: A colleague from the university's logistics office who handles contracts keeps coming to the canteen at lunch to check things with you. Later the two of you walk along the Qinhuai River for a whole evening, and only then do you realize he didn't really need to check that many things.
events.e_noro: One winter students in several classes fall ill with upset stomachs one after another, and the disease control center comes to take samples. You guard the sample fridge and every record and cooperate for three days. The conclusion is that the canteen wasn't involved, and you sit outside your building a long time before going home.
events.e_cert: The company sends you to qualify as a HACCP internal auditor: three days of classes and an exam. You come back with the certificate, and the first thing you do is redraw the critical control points for the cold-dish room.
events.e_ai_temp: The canteen installs wireless temperature probes: the cold store, the sample fridge and the hot-holding counters upload every five minutes and alert your phone when out of range. You no longer copy out temperatures one by one, but you get woken up a few more times at night.
events.e_camera_ai: The open-kitchen cameras are hooked up to AI: no mask, no cap, playing on a phone, and it snaps a picture and pushes it to you automatically. Forty-odd alerts a day, more than half false, and you have to open every one.
events.e_wedding: You get married, and at the banquet you can't help checking whether every dish is cooked through. The head chef sends a red envelope through a friend, with a note tucked inside: stop staring at the food.
events.e_contract: The university re-tenders the canteen contract, and the company very nearly loses it. For three months you keep the logs and corrective records even more carefully than usual, and on the day of evaluation, the books the university's logistics office spends longest on are those.
events.e_baby: After your child is born you put labels on the home fridge separating raw from cooked. Your family laughs at you, saying nobody inspects you at home.
events.e_supplier: You go out to the suburbs to audit a tofu supplier and see standing water and flies around their cooling tanks. You mark it a fail on the audit form. When you get back someone calls to pull strings, and you don't answer.
events.e_short_staff: The kitchen can't hire, and most who come are women in their fifties and sixties, some who can barely read. You redo the checklists as pictures, red ticks and green crosses, and post them at every station.
events.e_graduation: Graduation season, and a senior writes on the canteen message wall: four years and never once a bad stomach from here, thank you to the kitchen. You take a photo and show it to no one.
events.e_knee: The kitchen floor is always wet, and you go up and down the stairs dozens of times a day. Your knees go first. The doctor says the meniscus is worn and to climb fewer stairs.
events.e_parent: Your mother is in hospital back home in Yancheng, and you take a week off. When the hospital meal arrives, the first thing you do is check if it's hot.
events.e_ai_report: The company's system can now score and rank the inspection records of a dozen canteens automatically and produce the monthly report. You go from staying up late writing monthly reports to checking the one AI wrote, catching where it counted an absence as a failure to fix a problem.
events.e_mentor: An on-site safety officer you trained holds out against a head chef on her own for the first time, sending back a batch of substandard eggs. She messages you: my hands were shaking, but I said it.
events.e_system: The canteen food safety manual you led the writing of is rolled out by the company to more than twenty projects in other provinces. When a new project opens, the first book handed out is that one.

c_say_no.title: Stop this dish or not
c_say_no.situation: Ten minutes before lunch opens, you check the core temperature of a pot of braised chicken: only sixty-two degrees. The head chef says it'll be done any second, and students are already lining up. By the rules you can stop it, but if this pot stops, four windows sit empty for ten minutes.

options.label: Stop it and send it back to the pot
options.result: You stop it. A long line forms at the windows; the manager comes over and asks one question, and you hold up the thermometer for him to see. The head chef doesn't say a word while he puts it back on the heat.

options.label: Wait two minutes and test again
options.result: You stand by the pot, and two minutes later it reads seventy-five. You write both numbers in the record, and the head chef gives you a look.

c_more_canteens.title: Take on two more canteens, aiming for Regional Food Safety Supervisor
c_more_canteens.situation: The company has taken on two new canteens in Xianlin and is short of safety officers. They ask if you can cover three sites on your own, riding back and forth every day. Do it well, and next year you're first in line for Regional Food Safety Supervisor.

options.label: Cover three sites
options.result: You ride twenty kilometers a day between three canteens, staggering the health checks. After six months all three are in the top three for inspection scores.

options.label: Hold on to one site
options.result: You say one person can't watch three sites; something will go wrong. The manager thinks it over and hires someone else. For a year, no one finds a fault in your site's records.

c_central_kitchen.title: Move to the company's new central kitchen
c_central_kitchen.situation: The company has built a central kitchen in Jiangning that delivers lunches to dozens of primary and middle schools, and needs a quality controller who knows HACCP. It's production lines, cold-chain trucks and tens of thousands of boxed meals a day: stricter procedures, ten-odd percent more pay, and work starts at three in the morning.

options.label: Go to the central kitchen
options.result: You trade one canteen kitchen for a line of stainless steel. The temperature you watch hardest is the chilling room before dawn, where things are most likely to go wrong.

options.label: Stay at the university canteen
options.result: You say you like the sight of students lining up at the windows. A colleague from the central kitchen says you should still come and look at their boxed meals sometime.

c_ai_flow.title: Design the daily routine of sensors plus AI alerts
c_ai_flow.situation: The company wants to roll out 'equipment temperature monitoring plus AI alerts plus human review' at every canteen, and is looking for an on-site officer to lead the procedure: which alerts need someone there in person, which can be checked remotely. Some say this means one officer will cover five canteens in future, and there'll be fewer jobs.

options.label: Lead the procedure
options.result: You turn every temperature anomaly you've seen over the years into a rule, and spell out which things AI can only flag and someone must go see. After it goes live, the night-time wake-up calls drop by half.

options.label: Just do your own site well
options.result: You say you'll look after your own canteen. Someone at headquarters writes the procedure; there are a few rules you think are wrong, and you say so in the group chat.

c_regional.title: Compete for Regional Food Safety Supervisor
c_regional.situation: The company is naming a Regional Food Safety Supervisor for the Jiangning area to run inspections, complaints and supplier audits across seven canteens. You have to submit a risk analysis for the area and defend it in front of several project managers, some of whom you would then be inspecting.

options.label: Put your name in
options.result: Your risk analysis names the one step most likely to go wrong at each canteen. During the defense one project manager says that's his canteen you're describing. You say yes, it's yours.

options.label: Not yet; wait a while
options.result: You don't think you can stand up to those project managers yet, and don't apply. In the new supervisor's first month, she comes to your site and goes through your logs.

c_auditor.title: Become a food safety auditor at a certification body
c_auditor.situation: A certification body is hiring auditors for catering systems, with front-line experience and an internal auditor certificate required. You'd no longer get up at five; you'd travel by project and audit other people's systems in other people's kitchens, for about the same pay.

options.label: Become an auditor
options.result: Checklist in hand, you walk into someone else's kitchen for the first time, and the first thing you look at is still the color of the cutting boards.
options.end: You became a food safety auditor, going through records, cold stores and staff in one unfamiliar kitchen after another. In the place others think is cleanest, you can always find a glue trap that needs changing.

options.label: Stay in contract catering
options.result: You say you still like watching over one place every day. The woman from the certification body leaves a card, and you tuck it into your HACCP certificate.

c_director.title: Become the company's Catering Food Safety Director
c_director.situation: By regulation, a company this size has to have a food safety director who reports to the boss at a monthly review and is the first to be held accountable if something happens. The boss asks if you'll take it: your signature will weigh differently, and you'll spend less and less time in the canteens.

options.label: Take the director post
options.result: On the first of every month you sit across from the boss and go through the risks page by page. Once you recommend dropping a supplier; the boss frowns, and finally nods.

options.label: Stay in the region
options.result: You say you want a few more years in the canteens. The company brings in a director from outside, who often calls on you in meetings to ask what's really happening in the region.

c_hometown.title: Go back home to Yancheng
c_hometown.situation: Your parents are getting old. A classmate in Yancheng says the nutrition canteen at a city hospital is hiring a food safety manager: thirty percent less pay, ten minutes from home. Your child is in school in Nanjing, so you'd be going back and forth.

options.label: Go back to Yancheng
options.result: You hand over your work in Nanjing and go home. The hospital canteen is smaller than the university's, and patients' meals have to be softer and blander.
options.end: You manage food safety at a hospital nutrition canteen in your hometown, with a liquid diet now among each day's retained samples. After work you visit your parents and buy groceries on the way, and on weekends you go back to Nanjing to see your child.

options.label: Stay in Nanjing
options.result: You hire a caregiver for your parents and go back once a month. Your mother says the caregiver's cooking is too salty, and you say I'll cook when I'm back.

c_quality_head.title: Become Head of Quality for the catering group
c_quality_head.situation: The company is acquired by a large catering group, which wants one person to run the quality and food safety system across hundreds of contract catering projects nationwide. That means half the year away, in meetings with investors, regulators and major clients.

options.label: Take it
options.result: You fly across most of China, and at every new project's kickoff you say the same thing: get the morning health checks right first.

options.label: Hand it to someone younger
options.result: You recommend a supervisor you trained. The first thing she calls to ask after taking over is how to check the sample fridge at a canteen in another province.

endings.retire: On your last day you go back to that university canteen. At half past five in the morning a young safety officer stands at the changing-room door, checking hands, asking questions, ticking boxes. You don't go in. You watch from the doorway a while, then get a cup of soy milk and a steamed bun, pause at the sample cabinet, and sit down to eat slowly.
endings.burnout: That winter, stairs are hard on your knees, and after months of early mornings several numbers on your checkup are in red. The company moves you to headquarters for training and records, nine to five. When you teach new hires, the first slide is still the cutting boards in five colors.

stages: You guard one canteen on your own. The daily controls run from health checks, receiving and samples all the way through to dishwashing and closing, with the infrared thermometer, disinfectant strips and core thermometer in the pockets of your whites; once a week you lead the shift heads through an inspection, photograph the problems into the group chat and chase them until they're fixed. The head chef is thirty years older than you, and you have to learn to say no politely.

You oversee seven canteens in the Jiangning area. Every day you ride to two or three sites, looking not only at the kitchens but at whether the on-site officers' records are real; student complaints, meetings with the universities and on-site supplier audits all land on you. When you sign a corrective notice, the project manager has to reply. Going from guarding one site to inspecting others', you have to choose your words more carefully.

You are the company's food safety director, reporting to the boss at the monthly review and going round every project each quarter. On your desk are the risk control list, the supplier roster and the incident response plan; what you approve is whether to drop a supplier or put a project under correction. When regulators summon the company, you're the one across the table. You rarely use a thermometer now; what you hold is report after signed report.

What you set now is the food safety system for hundreds of projects across the group: manuals, training, assessments, audits. Half your week is on the road, speaking at new project kickoffs, answering questions at clients' tender briefings, arguing for a testing budget at the group's quality committee. When you do visit a canteen, you still go to the sample fridge first.
work: A new prep cook takes the red board he used for raw chicken and starts cutting cucumbers on it. You stop him on the spot, tip out the bowl of cucumbers, and walk him through the five colored boards one by one.

The delivery driver says the truck's refrigeration broke down on the way. You probe the frozen shrimp: minus five. You write rejected on the receiving note, and the driver spends half an hour on the phone beside the truck.

The dishwasher's gauge has read eighty-two degrees the whole time, but you don't trust it, and hold a thermometer to the outlet: sixty-eight. The day you report it for repair, you switch to manual sanitizing.

At a canteen in Xianlin, three days of the on-site officer's sample logs are in exactly the same handwriting. You check the timestamps against the camera footage and talk with her all afternoon. She cries and says she's too tired to keep up.

You audit a new vegetable supplier, going through case after case in their sorting shed with twenty strips of pesticide residue rapid tests, and when you're done you write on the audit report: conditional pass.

A student's parent posts online that their child got sick from canteen food. You pull that day's samples, temperature records and footage and write an incident statement, and the university's logistics office reads it and says they'll reply with that.
The boss wants to switch to a meat supplier twenty percent cheaper. You print that supplier's spot-check records for the past two years and put them on his desk, with a red circle on page three.
You run a company-wide food poisoning drill, from sealing samples to reporting to disease control, every project manager holding a procedure card while you stand at the back with a stopwatch.

The market regulator summons the company because one project was found with expired health certificates. You go with the corrective report and explain clearly what happened and how it's being fixed, and how it will be checked every month from now on.

The group has taken on the canteen at a large hospital in another province, and you take two people for the pre-opening review. You stand at the cold-store door for an hour and require the shelves to be moved another ten centimeters from the wall.
At a tender briefing, a major client asks how you keep standards the same across hundreds of canteens. You put the group's audit data on the screen and walk them through it project by project.

The AI system ranks risk across all the group's projects nationwide, and last place goes to a small canteen in the west. You don't send a corrective notice straight away; you fly out first and eat there for three days.
past: You go to middle school in Yancheng, where your family runs a small restaurant. You've helped in the kitchen since you were little, washing dishes and picking over vegetables, and what you hate most is the flies in summer.

Your gaokao (college entrance exam) score isn't high. You think about studying cooking, but your mother says don't be a cook, learn to manage the cooks. You put down food quality and safety at a vocational college in Nanjing.

In microbiology lab you see, for the first time, the colonies grown in a petri dish from a swab of a cutting board, patch after patch. You go home and tell your mother our dishcloths need boiling every day.
You intern on the store management team at a fast-food chain, copying temperatures, sticking labels and checking dates every day. The store manager says you're too fussy; customers can't wait.

After graduation you join this contract caterer and are posted to the management team at the university canteen, copying records and learning sampling under the previous safety officer, running errands and doing odd jobs.

The previous safety officer is moved to the central kitchen. You take the training and assessment for food safety management staff, and the day you pass, the manager hands you the key to the sample fridge.

late.pension_note: Estimate: thirty-odd years of contributions to Nanjing's basic pension for company employees at your wage base comes to a little over forty percent of your final monthly pay, plus a small company annuity from your later years at the group.
scenes: For the first few months of retirement you still wake a little after five. You get up and reorganize the fridge at home: raw on the bottom, cooked on top.
The senior canteen in your neighborhood asks you to be an adviser, twice a week, to look over the kitchen. Your first written suggestion: label the sample boxes with the date.
Your child gets into university and sends you a photo of the first meal in the canteen. You zoom in to see whether the cooks behind the window are wearing caps.
You're sunning yourself on a bench under the plane trees when the old woman beside you says her grandson got sick from his university canteen. You say, ask him which meal it was.
At headquarters you work nine to five and no longer get up at five. The first morning you take your child to school, you stand at the gate a long time.
A young on-site safety officer calls: the head chef won't let her stop a delivery. You hear her out and say only: write down the temperature, and I'll go with you to talk to him.
When the time comes you retire. Clearing your desk, you find a stack of the picture checklists you drew, red ticks and green crosses, and keep one.
In your first year out of contract catering, whenever you eat out, you still glance first at whether the kitchen door has a rodent guard.
You find your footing in the new place. On a trip back to Jiangning you see the university canteen has been renovated, with the open-kitchen feed scrolling on a big screen at the entrance.
A safety officer you trained becomes a regional supervisor and sends you a photo: her explaining cutting-board colors to new hires, in exactly the words you used.
Later the canteens fill up with cameras and probes, and when an alert sounds, it's all clear on the phone. But whether a pot of meat is cooked, someone still has to push a thermometer in.

Your granddaughter asks if you used to be a chef. You say no, you managed the chefs. She asks if that meant you got to eat first every day, and you laugh and say every meal, you had to set one portion aside first.

closing.retire: One autumn many years later you pass a middle school just at lunchtime, the smell of food drifting from the canteen windows. You stand outside the wall breathing it in a while, find nothing wrong, and walk slowly on.
closing.burnout: Many years later you find in a drawer the core thermometer you used for so many years, its battery long dead. You wipe it clean and put it back in its box.
closing.end: Many years later, cooking for your family, you finish cutting raw meat and switch boards without thinking. Your grandson asks why, and you say habit, then wash the board clean and stand it up beside the sink.
